title: Java Enterprise & JVM Architecture
description: Tests Java memory models, JVM garbage collection, concurrency primitives, Stream APIs, and object-oriented contracts.

questions.question: Where are local primitive variables and object instances allocated respectively in standard JVM architecture?
options: Primitives on the Stack frame; Object instances on the Heap.
Both primitives and object instances are allocated exclusively in the Metaspace.
Primitives on the Heap; Object instances in CPU registers.
Both are allocated in the permanent generation (PermGen).
questions.explanation: Local variables and primitive values inside method calls reside in the Thread Stack frame. All actual object instances, regardless of where they are instantiated, are allocated in the shared Heap memory.

questions.question: What is the result of comparing strings created with literals versus the 'new' keyword?
options: true true
true false
false false
false true
questions.explanation: String literals are stored in the JVM String Constant Pool and reused, so s1 and s2 share the same memory reference (s1 == s2 is true). The 'new' keyword explicitly allocates a distinct object instance on the heap (s1 == s3 is false).

questions.question: What is the crucial contract between the equals() and hashCode() methods in Java Collections?
options: If two objects are equal according to equals(), they must produce the identical integer hashCode().
If two objects have the same hashCode(), they are guaranteed to return true on equals().
Both methods must be declared final in all subclasses.
hashCode() must always return a positive 64-bit integer.
questions.explanation: The Java language contract states: If o1.equals(o2) is true, then o1.hashCode() must equal o2.hashCode(). The reverse is not required, as different objects can produce identical hash codes (hash collision).

questions.question: What guarantees does declaring a field 'volatile' provide in the Java Memory Model (JMM)?
options: It provides full mutual exclusion locks similar to a synchronized block.
It guarantees visibility of writes across threads and prevents instruction reordering around the read/write.
It causes the field to be serialized automatically across network sockets.
It prevents the variable from ever being modified after initialization.
questions.explanation: The volatile modifier guarantees that all reads and writes go directly to main memory rather than thread-local CPU caches, establishing a happens-before relationship and preventing compiler/CPU reordering.

questions.question: Why does Java utilize 'Type Erasure' for its Generics implementation?
options: To allow generic types to be dynamically converted into Python bytecode at runtime.
To maintain backward compatibility with legacy non-generic Java bytecode compiled prior to Java 5.
To prevent objects from being inspected using reflection.
To enforce that all generic classes are strictly final.
questions.explanation: Java generics were introduced in Java 5. Type erasure removes type parameters during compilation (replacing them with Object or bounds) so that the generated bytecode remained fully binary-compatible with older JVMs.

questions.question: In Java 8+ Streams, which of the following operations is a Terminal operation that triggers stream evaluation?
options: map()
filter()
distinct()
collect()
questions.explanation: Intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted, distinct) are lazy and only construct a stream pipeline. Terminal operations (collect, forEach, reduce, count) initiate computation and produce a final result or side effect.

questions.question: How does Java resolve conflicts when a class implements two interfaces containing identical default method signatures?
options: The JVM arbitrarily picks interface A because it was listed first in the implements clause.
The code compiles but throws a MethodResolutionException at runtime.
The compiler throws an error unless the implementing class explicitly overrides and resolves the method.
Interface B always overrides interface A by convention.
questions.explanation: Java prevents diamond problem ambiguity by requiring the implementing class to provide its own implementation of the conflicting method, optionally calling A.super.execute() or B.super.execute().

questions.question: Why is ConcurrentHashMap significantly more scalable in multithreaded environments than Collections.synchronizedMap()?
options: It stores all keys on external SSD storage instead of RAM.
It uses fine-grained locking with compare-and-swap (CAS) and synchronized node buckets rather than locking the entire map for every operation.
It converts all put operations into asynchronous JMS messages.
It ignores write conflicts by dropping concurrent mutations.
questions.explanation: Synchronized map wraps operations in a single coarse-grained lock, serializing all thread access. ConcurrentHashMap permits high concurrent read throughput without locking, and locks only individual tree/bucket bins on write.

questions.question: Which of the following exception classes is an UNCHECKED exception in Java?
options: java.io.IOException
java.sql.SQLException
java.lang.NullPointerException
java.lang.ClassNotFoundException
questions.explanation: Unchecked exceptions inherit from java.lang.RuntimeException (or Error). NullPointerException, IndexOutOfBoundsException, and IllegalArgumentException do not require explicit throws clauses or try-catch blocks.

questions.question: What interface must an object implement to be eligible for automatic resource cleanup in a try-with-resources statement?
options: java.lang.Runnable
java.io.Serializable
java.lang.AutoCloseable
java.lang.Cloneable
questions.explanation: Any class implementing java.lang.AutoCloseable (or its subinterface java.io.Closeable) can be declared in a try-with-resources statement, ensuring its close() method is called automatically upon completion.
